paragraphs.heading: A far-seeing tool
paragraphs.text: A telescope is a device for observing distant objects through the electromagnetic radiation they give off, absorb or reflect. The name comes from Ancient Greek words for 'far' and 'to look', so a telescope is literally 'far-seeing'. At first the word meant an optical instrument built with lenses, curved mirrors or both. Today it covers a wide range of instruments that pick up different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, and in some cases other kinds of detectors.

paragraphs.heading: The first telescopes
paragraphs.text: The first known practical telescopes were refracting telescopes, made with glass lenses, and they appeared in the Netherlands at the start of the 17th century. They were used both for looking around on Earth and for astronomy. The oldest surviving record is a 1608 patent filed by Hans Lipperhey, a spectacle maker from Middelburg, although nobody knows who really invented it. Word spread across Europe, and in 1609 Galileo built his own and turned it on objects in the sky. The word "telescope" was coined in 1611 by Giovanni Demisiani for one of Galileo's instruments.

paragraphs.heading: Mirrors instead of lenses
paragraphs.text: Soon after the refractor appeared, people began asking whether the objective, the part that gathers light, could be a mirror rather than a lens. Parabolic mirrors promised less spherical aberration and no chromatic aberration, which led to many proposed designs. The first practical reflecting telescope was built by Isaac Newton in 1668, and the design now carries his name as the Newtonian reflector. Early reflectors used speculum metal mirrors that tarnished fast, a problem eased when glass mirrors coated with silver arrived in 1857, and aluminized ones in 1932.

paragraphs.heading: Why big telescopes use mirrors
paragraphs.text: Simple lenses had colour problems of their own, which the achromatic lens, invented in 1733, partly corrected. Even so, a refracting telescope can be at most about 1 metre across. As a result, nearly all the big optical telescopes built for research since about 1900 have been reflectors. The biggest today have objectives wider than 10 metres, and several 30–40m designs are in the works. Size matters because a larger aperture both collects more light and gives finer angular resolution.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond visible light
paragraphs.text: The 20th century brought telescopes for wavelengths from radio to gamma rays. The first purpose-built radio telescope started work in 1937, and infrared telescopes followed in the 1960s. Each band needs its own approach: at longer wavelengths antennas become easier to use, so in the far-infrared a telescope can work more like a radio telescope. Earth's atmosphere blocks most of the spectrum, letting through only visible and near-infrared light and part of the radio range. That is why there are no X-ray or far-infrared telescopes on the ground.

paragraphs.heading: Telescopes in space
paragraphs.text: Even where light does reach the ground, clouds, astronomical seeing and light pollution can make orbit a better home. The drawbacks of a space telescope are cost, size, and the difficulty of maintaining or upgrading it. NASA's Hubble Space Telescope detects visible, ultraviolet and near-infrared light, while the Kepler Space Telescope discovered thousands of exoplanets. The James Webb Space Telescope, launched on 25 December 2021 on an Ariane 5 rocket from Kourou in French Guiana, sees in infrared and circles the L₂ Lagrange Point of the Earth–Sun system.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting telescopes
paragraphs.text: Telescopes can also be grouped by where they work: on the ground, in space, or flying. They can be grouped by who uses them, professional or amateur astronomers. A permanent campus or a vehicle housing telescopes or other instruments, one or many, is called an observatory.
